newsitem.title: USA: Republicans enter budget round with image problem.
newsitem.headline: Republicans enter budget round with image problem.

text.p: Congressional Republicans head into negotiations to forge final tax and spending legislation with a scarred public image from White House attacks on the fairness of their plans, analysts said Monday.

House and Senate negotiators planned to begin meetings Thursday and Friday to resolve differences in their separate spending and tax bills. The goal was to vote on a final product at the end of July and send it to President Clinton before the congressional August recess.
While the "conference" to reconcile differences is a regular part of the budget-making process, this year's emphasis on bipartisanship and working with the White House has added a new twist.

It began with the budget agreement in May between leaders of the Republican-dominated Congress and Clinton, a Democrat, to wipe out the budget deficit over five years and give Americans $85 billion in net tax cuts.

"This is going to be not so much a dance involving the House and the Senate, but more one involving the White House and the Congress," Robert Reischauer, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, said.
The White House has voiced opposition to provisions in the House and Senate bills and has put forward its own tax plan.

The Clinton administration is trying to paint the House and Senate tax bills as giving too much of a tax break to the wealthy. Republicans say their tax cuts mostly benefit the middle class and accuse Democrats of wanting to give money back to people who do not pay taxes.

"If they're (Republicans) going to win ... they're going to have to be willing to take on the class warfare argument that seems to be carrying the day in this whole tax debate right now," Stephen Moore, director of fiscal policy studies at the Cato Institute, said.
"Unless Republicans can convince the public that this tax bill is not about redistributing wealth but about creating wealth, they're going to lose," Moore said.

Republicans also must contend with internal tension from conservatives who say the party has given too much to the president and should just work out differences between the House and Senate without White House input, Reischauer said.
"I think the president is in a remarkably good position," Reischauer said, adding that Republicans made two big mistakes.

The Republican tactic on the disaster relief bill misfired when Clinton vetoed the legislation and in the end got what he originally wanted, Reischauer said. Republicans also erred by not working out some key differences between the House and Senate spending and tax bills ahead of time so they could present a "united front" to White House objections, he said.
"They (Republicans) can't compete on the bully pulpit with the president," Reischauer said. "He speaks with a single voice."

Pivotal battles in the coming tax bill talks include indexing capital gains so investors are not taxed on profits from investments attributed to inflation, Moore said. Conservatives were maintaining pressure to keep that provision in the final bill, while Clinton strongly opposes indexing, which is in the House tax bill but not in the Senate version.

Conservatives want the capital gains tax reduced to a maximum 20 percent rate from the current 28 percent to be in the final tax bill, Moore said. Clinton has proposed excluding 30 percent of investment profits from the capital gains tax, which would not cut the top rate by much, Moore said.

"Out of all the bottom lines, that is the bottom line," Moore said. "If Republicans didn't win on that, then I really do think you would have a whole number of the pro-growth wing of the Republican party say 'What's left in this budget deal for our side?'."
